Linked all 18 assertions from the 1860 and 1880 Joseph Pratt households to the existing tree persons, at `confident` on every link.

Links written (20 `pe_` entries, pe_001 to pe_020):
- **1860 household (src_001):** Joseph (head) to I1, Ann to I2, Sarah to I3, Joseph (son, age 10) to I4. Each persona scored 0.78 with `same_person`.
- **1880 household (src_002):** Joseph (head) to I1, Ann to I2, Joseph (son, age 30) to I4. Each scored 0.78. The two relationship assertions also bear on the other party, so "wife of Joseph Pratt" and "son of Joseph Pratt" each have a second link to I1, scored with the head role.

Basis for the tier:
- Ages agree with the tree's birth years for all four people in both censuses (gap 0 years each).
- Birthplace England agrees with the tree.
- The household composition matches the tree's family.
- The move from Cranfield, England (1851) to Salt Lake County, Utah is about 7,767 km. The Utah emigration wiki page says "Many Latter-day Saint immigrants leaving Europe and Great Britain came on chartered ships from Liverpool, England." That sentence names the prior country with an arrival verb in the 1840 to 1890 era, so it bridges the move. I quoted it in each entry's `move_bridge` field.

Materialization: facts from both censuses were written onto I1 through I4 with source references. No conflicts surfaced.

Open points:
- **Sarah (I3) is absent from the 1880 household.** She would be about 33 then. Nothing in the tree marks her as dead, so this is an identity question (death, marriage elsewhere, or enumeration elsewhere), not a conflict. It is noted in the I1 rationale.
- `person_warnings` reports one "implausible" nonStandardPlace warning per person (I1 to I4). These come from the 1841 and 1851 Cranfield residence facts that were already in the tree, not from this run. They are unresolved and need a place-standardization pass.
- The question q_001 (are these households the subject's family) is answered only on identity. The household links support it, but the Sarah absence should be checked before it is closed.

Sarah does not appear in the 1880 household, so the next step is to find out where she was that year, which will settle whether this is the same family.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

output.text_response:
**Verdict: `confident` is not justified on pe_005. The calibrated tier is `probable`, and the rationale needs rewriting.** No changes were made to research.json or tree.gedcomx.json.

---

## What pe_005 rests on

- **Name:** "Patrick Flynn" matches tree person I1, but this is a common name and carries little weight alone.
- **Death date and place:** These agree with I1's Death fact (1908-03-12, Schuylkill County). However, that Death fact was sourced to S3 — *this same death certificate*. The agreement is **circular** and cannot confirm identity.
- **Residence:** The rationale says the death location "matches known residence." That residence comes from the 1850 and 1860 census links (pe_001, pe_004), which *are* independent. This is the one non-circular point in the link's favour.
- **Father:** "Father: Thomas Flynn" (a_013) matches I2 in the tree. This is the only identity-bearing element unique to this record — but the informant is a son-in-law reporting hearsay about his father-in-law's parentage (secondary hearsay, one evidence unit).
- **Age:** No age assertion is in the record; only an approximate birth year (~1845), which is compatible but does not strengthen the link.
- **Birthplace:** The certificate says Pennsylvania; the tree has Ireland. Conflict c_001 resolves this in favour of Ireland, so it doesn't block the link, but the birth facts cannot corroborate identity here.

---

## Calibration problems

1. **Wrong tier:** The `confident` (Strong) tier requires name, age, place, and relationship to agree on *independent* grounds. Place agreement is circular, age is absent, and the relationship fit rests on secondary hearsay. This is **Moderate**, warranting `probable`.
2. **Incomplete rationale:** Missing required elements — the date check (gap ~0 years, compatible), the residence check (Schuylkill County vs. census-anchored residence, with distance if applicable), the score disclosure, and an acknowledgement of the circular death fact.
3. **match_score is null** with no explanation; the rationale doesn't say why a `same_person` score was not obtained.
4. **Unlinked party:** Thomas Flynn (I2) is named in the father assertion but has no `pe_` link to a_013. Under the both-sided rule, I2 should receive a `speculative` link given the hearsay source.

---

## Recommended actions (need your authorization)

1. Downgrade pe_005's confidence from `confident` → `probable`.
2. Rewrite the rationale to cover: name match; circularity of the death-fact agreement; census-anchored residence; father match as hearsay from a son-in-law informant; date check; residence check; score status; and the settled birthplace conflict (c_001).
3. Add a `speculative` link from a_013 to I2 (Thomas Flynn) with its own rationale.

Would you like to proceed with any of these changes?

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The 1875 San Francisco Great Register entry for Hermann Gatjen has been linked to tree person I1 (Hermann) at **probable** confidence. Here is the full result:

**Identity Decision: Probable (score 0.43)**
The name matches (Gatjen = Gaetjen spelling variant), the register's age of 21 gives a birth year of ~1854 which is close to the tree's unsourced "about 1859," Germany agrees with the 1871 index's Prussia, and San Francisco fits the family setting. No contradictions exist in the tree data. Probable is the ceiling because name, age, and place are the only corroborating elements.

**Nine person_evidence links written** (a_001 through a_009) for all assertions in the register, all at probable confidence.

**Naturalization shortfall flagged:** The 1871 arrival to the 13 August 1875 naturalization is only ~4 years 2 months, short of the 5-year residency requirement. No explanation appears in the project. Both the naturalization link and the existing arrival link are capped at probable as a result.

**Conflicts surfaced (not resolved):**
- Two birth years are now on Hermann's record: the unsourced "about 1859" and the register-derived "~1854." Conflict-resolution should determine which stands.

**No separate stub needed** — the evidence is sufficient to link to I1, though at probable rather than confident.

**Question q_001 not yet answered:** The register says only "Germany" — it does not name a specific origin. The next recommended step is the California 4th District Court naturalization record from 13 August 1875, which could both confirm the naturalization date, resolve the shortfall puzzle, and potentially identify a more specific German place of origin.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

"Herm" is almost certainly an index truncation of "Hermann"; the underlying manifest's spelling cannot be verified without the original record. Identity of this passenger with tree subject I1 (Hermann Gaetjen, born ~1859) is uncertain: the stated birth year 1854 differs from the tree subject's approximate birth year by five years. This identity question must be resolved by corroborating evidence, not asserted from this index alone.

Birth year 1854 as stated in the index conflicts with the tree subject I1's approximate birth year of ~1859 — a five-year discrepancy that raises an identity question. Notably, the 1875 San Francisco Great Register entry (src_001) records a Hermann Gatjen aged 21, implying birth ~1854, which is consistent with this index entry; the two may record the same individual. Whether that individual is the same as tree subject I1 requires independent corroboration. The birth year in a passenger index would typically derive from the passenger's self-reported age or a birth year column on the original manifest; neither can be verified without the original.

Prussia is a broad political designation covering a large territory, not a specific locality. It does not identify a German province, town, or parish of origin. The index records no departure port or ship name, so the original manifest — which may carry a more specific origin — cannot be located from this entry alone.

review_dimensions.name: Rationale quality
review_dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites specific matching attributes: name (William, Mary, James, Ellen, George), age (gap 0 years for each), English birthplace, household composition (wife Mary, children James, Ellen, George present in 1870), and relationship roles (son, daughter, wife). The geographic gap is explicitly named in every rationale: both places, the 6,804 km distance, the absence of a corridor on the Tennessee page, and the absence of a documentary bridge in the project. The 1880 rationales note the absence of James and Ellen and flag it as an identity question. Competing candidates are implicitly ruled out by the household match across two independent censuses.

review_dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
review_dimensions.rationale: All relationship assertions are linked to both parties. The 1880 wife assertion (a_019) is linked to I2 (pe_019) and to I1 as the head (pe_020). The 1880 son assertion (a_020) is linked to I5 (pe_021) and to I1 as the father (pe_022). Each relationship-implying assertion has two person_evidence entries, one for each person in the relationship. No relationship is linked to only one side.

review_dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
review_dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all five tree persons (I1–I5) already existed. The skill linked assertions to existing persons and materialized facts onto them via materialize_facts, which enriched existing facts with source references. The household edges (R1–R7) already existed in the tree from the 1851 and 1861 English censuses and were not re-written, which is correct: the skill does not re-write edges already on file. No new edges were required because the household skeleton was already complete. The scenario did not involve unmatched personas or missing household members, so minting was not applicable.

review_dimensions.name: Score discipline
review_dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every persona-candidate pair: CP1–CP5 (1870) and DP1–DP3 (1880) against I1–I5. Each call returned a score of 0.78, which was recorded in match_score and informed the confidence decision. The score was not allowed to override the geographic cap: despite the high score, confidence remained 'probable' because the unexplained move outside the residence cluster is a qualitative constraint independent of the score.
